people.name: Ruth Nomura Tanbara
body: In August 1942, months after President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066, Ruth and Earl Tanbara arrived in St. Paul. On the West Coast, people of Japanese ancestry were being forcibly removed and confined in camps. The Minnesota Historical Society's MNopedia describes the Tanbaras as the first Japanese Americans to resettle in St. Paul as a result of the order.

Ruth Tokuko Nomura was born in Portland, Oregon, on October 15, 1907, to immigrant (Issei) parents, which made her Nisei, the American-born second generation. In 1930 she earned a degree in home economics from Oregon State Agricultural College, now Oregon State University, where she was the first Nisei woman from Portland to enroll. In 1935 she married Earl K. Tanbara and moved to Berkeley, California.

In March 1942 the couple left Berkeley for a friend's farm in Reedley, California, and in July they received War Relocation Authority permission to move to St. Paul. When they arrived, they reported to the International Institute of St. Paul with letters of introduction and offered to help other Japanese Americans being relocated. They joined the St. Paul Resettlement Committee, which the International Institute had formed, and Ruth gave public talks to build acceptance. Within three years the couple assisted more than 100 families. They stayed in St. Paul after the war.

Ruth joined the St. Paul YWCA's program staff, where she directed adult education classes and the international program, and retired in 1972 after 30 years. In 1953 she earned a master of science degree in adult education from the University of Minnesota. In 1973 the YWCA dedicated a Japanese garden in her honor. She also started the effort that became Reflections: Memoirs of Japanese American Women in Minnesota, published in 1994, which kept a record of women's resettlement experiences. She died in Afton, Minnesota, on January 4, 2008, at age 100.
keyFacts: 1907: Born October 15 in Portland, Oregon.
1930: Degree in home economics, Oregon State Agricultural College.
August 1942: Resettled in St. Paul; with Earl, helped more than 100 families within three years.
1972: Retired after 30 years on the St. Paul YWCA program staff.
1994: Reflections: Memoirs of Japanese American Women in Minnesota published.
2008: Died January 4 in Afton, Minnesota.
people.connectToWork: When someone arrives in Minnesota because a government forced the move, how would your intake or planning conversation change if you asked what they left and who helped them here?

people.name: John Fujio Aiso
people.field: Military intelligence, law and the judiciary
body: In 1941 John Aiso, a Harvard-trained lawyer, was a drafted private working in the motor pool at Camp Hahn in Riverside, California. Army officers looking for Japanese-language talent selected him for the Army's new language school. He rose from student to assistant instructor to head instructor, and later became director of training at the Army's secret Japanese-language school, the institution that brought thousands of Nisei soldiers to Minnesota.

Aiso was born December 14, 1909, in Burbank, California, and graduated from Brown University and Harvard Law School. The school opened at the Presidio of San Francisco on November 1, 1941. After Japanese Americans were removed from the West Coast it could no longer stay in California. Minnesota offered a home, and in June 1942 it restarted at Camp Savage with 18 instructors and 200 students. It became the Military Intelligence Service Language School, with a staff that grew to more than 150. It moved to Fort Snelling in August 1944 and left Minnesota for Monterey, California, in 1946.

More than 6,000 military intelligence specialists had graduated when the school closed in Minnesota in 1946, most of them Nisei. Many had family members held in incarceration camps even as they trained to translate documents and question prisoners in the Pacific.

After the war Aiso returned to law. In 1952 he was named a Los Angeles Municipal Court judge, described as the first Nisei to hold a U.S. judicial post. He became a Superior Court judge in 1957, and in 1968 Governor Ronald Reagan elevated him to the California Court of Appeal, Second District. He retired in 1983. Honors include the Legion of Merit (1965), Japan's Order of the Rising Sun, Third Class (1984), and induction into the Military Intelligence Corps Hall of Fame (1991). The library at the Defense Language Institute bears his name. He died on December 29, 1987, about two weeks after he was attacked in a mugging in Hollywood.
keyFacts: 1909: Born December 14 in Burbank, California.
November 1, 1941: Language school opens at the Presidio of San Francisco.
June 1942: School reopens at Camp Savage, Minnesota; August 1944: moves to Fort Snelling; 1946: moves to Monterey.
More than 6,000 graduates in all; last Minnesota class June 1946.
1952: Los Angeles Municipal Court judge; 1968: California Court of Appeal.
1987: Died December 29.
people.connectToWork: Where does your agency rely on someone's skills or language while treating people like them with suspicion, and how would you find out?

people.name: Sally Sudo
body: In 1997 the Smithsonian exhibit "Whispered Silences," about the World War II camps, came to the downtown Minneapolis Public Library. Sally Sudo signed on as a docent. Talking with visitors, she found that many Minnesotans knew nothing about the camps, and that led her to spend her retirement telling her family's story.

Sudo was born Shigeyo Ohno on December 1, 1935, in Seattle, one of 10 children in a family in the city's Japantown (Nihonmachi). She was six when her family was forcibly removed under Executive Order 9066. They were held for about three and a half years, first at the Puyallup detention facility in Washington and then at the Minidoka camp in Idaho. Her brother Joe served in the Army's Military Intelligence Service and trained at Fort Snelling, and he helped bring the family to Minnesota after the camp closed.

She met her husband, an exchange student from Japan, at the University of Minnesota, and they raised three children. His work took the family to Japan for many years, and she taught there and in Minnesota. They returned to Minnesota in 1984.

She has spoken at schools, churches and community groups and chaired the education committee of the Twin Cities chapter of the Japanese American Citizens League. She staffed booths at teacher conferences such as the 2014 Minnesota Council for the Social Studies meeting, and in 2017 she joined a panel with CAIR-Minnesota on whether incarceration could happen again, this time to Muslim Americans. As of its April 2024 profile, the Coalition of Asian American Leaders described her as still speaking in retirement.
keyFacts: 1935: Born December 1 in Seattle.
Childhood: About three and a half years incarcerated at Puyallup and Minidoka with her family.
After the camp closed: Moved to Minnesota with help from her brother, a Military Intelligence Service veteran.
1984: Returned to Minnesota after many years in Japan.
1997: Docent for "Whispered Silences" in Minneapolis.
Chaired the Twin Cities JACL education committee.
people.connectToWork: What might an older person who was held by the government as a child want to know before sharing records or answering questions, and how would you make it easy for them to ask?

people.name: Edwin "Bud" Nakasone
body: On December 7, 1941, 14-year-old Bud Nakasone, at home in Hawaii near Wheeler Army Airfield, saw Japanese planes attack. In his own account, he was a recent Leilehua High School graduate of 18 when the Army drafted him on August 10, 1945, days before the war ended. By his own account in Discover Nikkei, he arrived at Fort Snelling on December 25, 1945, for the Military Intelligence Service Language School; MPR News (May 16, 2024) says he moved from Hawaii to Minnesota on Christmas Eve, 1947. Classes began in March 1946, and when the school moved to the Presidio of Monterey that July, his class moved with it. He then served as an interpreter in occupied Japan in 1947 and 1948.

Military Intelligence Service linguists translated captured documents, questioned prisoners and later worked between two cultures during the occupation. Their contributions stayed classified for decades, so most Americans did not learn about them for a long time.

Nakasone settled in Minnesota. He graduated from the University of Minnesota and became a high school teacher and then a longtime member of the history faculty at Century College in White Bear Lake. He continued in the Army on active duty and in the Reserve, and retired as a colonel after 41 years. As a historian he has written books and produced videos about World War II and the Japanese American experience, including The Nisei Soldier: Historical Essays on World War II and the Korean War (second revised edition, 1999).

In 1954 he married Mary, a University of Minnesota librarian. His son, Gen. Paul Nakasone, has said his father's Reserve career influenced his decision to join ROTC. In May 2024, MPR News reported Bud at a Fort Snelling ceremony honoring Minnesota's Japanese American veterans, attending with his son. In November 2025, Pioneer PBS featured father and son in Greater Good: Mission of a MN Family.
keyFacts: December 7, 1941: Saw the attack on Pearl Harbor at age 14.
August 10, 1945: Drafted into the Army.
December 25, 1945: Arrived at Fort Snelling, by his own account (MPR News gives Christmas Eve, 1947).
1947–1948: Interpreter during the occupation of Japan.
Longtime history faculty member at Century College, White Bear Lake.
Retired as an Army colonel after 41 years of active and Reserve service.
people.connectToWork: Which places in your region carry a history your team has not learned, and how might that history change the way you talk with the people connected to it?

people.name: Paul Miki Nakasone
body: In May 2018 a general from White Bear Lake, Minnesota, took charge of two of the nation's most powerful security organizations at once: the National Security Agency and U.S. Cyber Command. The general was Paul Nakasone, the son of a Nisei veteran who had trained as a military linguist at Fort Snelling.

His father, Edwin "Bud" Nakasone, was a Military Intelligence Service veteran and Army Reserve officer, and Paul has said that example drew him to ROTC. He graduated from Saint John's University in Collegeville, Minnesota, class of 1986. He later earned graduate degrees from the U.S. Army War College, the National Defense Intelligence College and the University of Southern California.

His first operational tour began in 1987 as an assistant intelligence officer at Fort Carson, Colorado. Over 37 years in the Army his posts included assistant brigade operations officer with the 35th Signal Brigade at Fort Bragg in 1992, and from October 2016 to April 2018 he commanded U.S. Army Cyber Command.

From May 2018 to February 2, 2024, he led the NSA and U.S. Cyber Command. In February 2024 the U.S. Senate entered a tribute into the Congressional Record honoring his retirement and his family's service. As of October 2026 he is founding director of Vanderbilt University's Institute of National Security and joined the board of the cybersecurity company Armadin that month.
keyFacts: Native of White Bear Lake, Minnesota.
1986: Saint John's University graduate.
1987: First operational tour at Fort Carson, Colorado.
2016–2018: Commander, U.S. Army Cyber Command.
May 2018 to February 2, 2024: Commander, U.S. Cyber Command, and Director, NSA.
As of October 2026: Founding director, Vanderbilt Institute of National Security.
people.connectToWork: When you meet a family whose story crosses generations of public service and public suspicion, what would you need to ask rather than assume about how they see government?

people.name: David Mura
people.field: Literature, poetry, memoir, race and identity
body: On a writing fellowship, a young Sansei poet (third-generation Japanese American) spent a year in Japan, his grandparents' homeland. The memoir he wrote about that year, Turning Japanese: Memoirs of a Sansei (1991), won the Josephine Miles Book Award from Oakland PEN and a 1991 Minnesota Book Award.

Mura was born June 17, 1952, and grew up in the Chicago area. He earned a B.A. in English from Grinnell College, did graduate work at the University of Minnesota, and later earned an MFA from Vermont College. He settled in the Twin Cities and built his career there.

His first poetry collection, After We Lost Our Way, was a National Poetry Series winner. The Colors of Desire, Angels for the Burning (2004) and The Last Incantations (2014) followed. His second memoir, Where the Body Meets Memory: An Odyssey of Race, Sexuality, and Identity (1995), explored his family's incarceration history and won another Minnesota Book Award in 1997. He also wrote the novel Famous Suicides of the Japanese Empire (2008), Songs for Uncle Tom, Tonto, and Mr. Moto: Poetry and Identity (2002), and A Stranger's Journey: Race, Identity, and Narrative Craft in Writing (2018).

Mura has also been a teacher and mentor. He served on the board of The Loft Literary Center in Minneapolis and taught poetry and creative nonfiction there. He and his wife, Susan Sencer, have three children, including a daughter who serves in the Minnesota House.
keyFacts: 1952: Born June 17; grew up in the Chicago area.
1991: Turning Japanese: Memoirs of a Sansei; Minnesota Book Award.
1995: Where the Body Meets Memory; Minnesota Book Award, 1997.
2018: A Stranger's Journey.
Teacher and board member at The Loft Literary Center, Minneapolis.
people.connectToWork: When someone's family history includes events they did not live through themselves, how would you make room for that in a conversation without asking them to explain or relive it?

people.name: Fred Toyosaburo Korematsu
body: On May 30, 1942, police arrested a young shipyard welder on a street corner in San Leandro, California. Fred Korematsu, an American citizen, had refused to report for the forced removal of Japanese Americans from the West Coast.

Korematsu was born January 30, 1919, in Oakland, California, to Japanese immigrant parents. He was convicted of violating the exclusion order and sent to camp, and he challenged the conviction to the U.S. Supreme Court. On December 18, 1944, in Korematsu v. United States, the Court ruled 6–3, in an opinion by Justice Hugo Black, to uphold the exclusion orders.

In the early 1980s researchers found that the government had suppressed evidence showing Japanese Americans posed no military threat. Using a rare legal procedure called coram nobis, which reopens a case because of fundamental error, Korematsu's legal team returned to court. On November 10, 1983, U.S. District Judge Marilyn Hall Patel vacated his conviction.

He spent the rest of his life speaking out for civil liberties. On January 15, 1998, President Bill Clinton awarded him the Presidential Medal of Freedom. He died March 30, 2005, at his daughter's home in Larkspur, California. In 2011 California observed the first Fred Korematsu Day on his birthday, the first day in the U.S. named for an Asian American.
keyFacts: 1919: Born January 30 in Oakland, California.
May 30, 1942: Arrested for refusing the exclusion order.
December 18, 1944: Korematsu v. United States, upheld 6–3.
November 10, 1983: Conviction vacated by Judge Marilyn Hall Patel.
January 15, 1998: Presidential Medal of Freedom.
January 30, 2011: First Fred Korematsu Day in California.
people.connectToWork: If a rule you apply today rested on information that later proved false, who would be able to tell you, and what would you do with it?

people.name: Patsy Takemoto Mink
body: In 1964 a lawyer from Hawaii won one of the state's two new at-large seats in the U.S. House of Representatives, taking 27 percent in a four-way race. Patsy Takemoto Mink became the first Asian American woman elected to Congress.

Mink was born December 6, 1927, in Paia, Maui, when Hawaii was a U.S. territory, into a Japanese American family. She graduated from Maui High School in 1944, attended Wilson College and the University of Nebraska, and earned a B.A. from the University of Hawaii in 1948. She received her law degree from the University of Chicago Law School in 1951.

Mink served in the House from 1965 to 1977. With Representative Edith Green and Senator Birch Bayh she built support for Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972, which bars sex discrimination in schools that receive federal funds. In 1975 she fought an amendment that would have exempted school athletics from Title IX.

She returned to Congress after winning a special election in September 1990 and served until her death on September 28, 2002, in Honolulu. On October 29, 2002, a joint resolution of Congress became law providing that Title IX may be cited as the "Patsy Takemoto Mink Equal Opportunity in Education Act." In 2014 President Barack Obama posthumously awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom.
keyFacts: 1927: Born December 6 in Paia, Maui.
1951: Law degree, University of Chicago.
1964: Elected to the U.S. House, the first Asian American woman in Congress.
1972: Helped win passage of Title IX.
2002: Died September 28; Title IX given a citation name in her honor.
2014: Posthumous Presidential Medal of Freedom.
people.connectToWork: Which protections do you and the people you serve rely on without knowing who fought for them, and what would it change to know that history when a protection is questioned?

people.name: Kristi Tsuya Yamaguchi
body: At the 1992 Winter Olympics in Albertville, France, a 20-year-old from Fremont, California, won the gold medal in women's figure skating.

Kristi Yamaguchi was born July 12, 1971, in Hayward, California, and grew up in Fremont. By U.S. Figure Skating's account, both sides of her family were incarcerated during World War II. Her mother's family, the Dois, was held at Amache in Granada, Colorado, while her grandfather George Doi served in the U.S. Army in Europe, and her mother, Carole, was born at Amache on January 1, 1945.

She won world championships in 1991 and 1992 along with her Olympic gold. In 1996 she founded the Always Dream Foundation, which has funded after-school programs, back-to-school clothing for children in need and summer camps for children with disabilities. She has also written Figure Skating for Dummies and children's books such as Dream Big, Little Pig! (2011) and It's a Big World, Little Pig! (2012). She was inducted into the U.S. Olympic Hall of Fame in 2005 and is a member of both the World and U.S. Figure Skating Halls of Fame.
keyFacts: 1971: Born July 12 in Hayward, California.
1991 and 1992: World figure skating champion.
1992: Olympic gold medal, Albertville, France.
1996: Founded the Always Dream Foundation.
2005: Inducted into the U.S. Olympic Hall of Fame.
people.connectToWork: If you heard only about someone's public success, what might you miss about their family's history with government, and how would you leave room for it to come up?

people.name: Isamu Noguchi
body: In 1942, about five months after Pearl Harbor and as the federal government forced Japanese Americans out of their West Coast homes, a sculptor already well known in New York went into the Poston camp in Arizona of his own free will. Isamu Noguchi lived on the East Coast, so Executive Order 9066 did not apply to him. He volunteered, hoping to teach art and help design the camp community.

Noguchi was born November 17, 1904, in Los Angeles. His father, Yone Noguchi, was a Japanese poet. His mother, Léonie Gilmour, was a white American writer who had worked as Yone's editorial assistant and translator. In 1907 his mother took him to Japan.

The camp did not turn out as he had hoped. Getting out took months longer than he expected, and he left after roughly six or seven months. Before the war he had made the stainless steel "News" plaque for the Associated Press Building at Rockefeller Center. He designed sets for the choreographer Martha Graham, including Appalachian Spring, which premiered at the Library of Congress on October 30, 1944. In 1947 he designed a three-sided glass coffee table for Herman Miller. In 1951, on a visit to Gifu, Japan, he reworked the city's paper lanterns into his Akari light sculptures. He also designed gardens, parks and playgrounds, including the UNESCO garden in Paris, and the Japanese American Community Center plaza in Los Angeles's Little Tokyo.

In 1985 he opened his own garden museum in New York City. He received the National Medal of Arts in 1987 and Japan's Order of the Sacred Treasure in 1988. He died in New York City on December 30, 1988.
keyFacts: 1904: Born November 17 in Los Angeles.
1942: Entered Poston camp voluntarily; stayed roughly six or seven months.
1947: Glass coffee table for Herman Miller.
1951: First Akari light sculptures.
1985: Opened his garden museum in New York City.
1987: National Medal of Arts; died December 30, 1988.
people.connectToWork: When a person's heritage crosses two or more countries, what form field, category or assumption at your work would not fit them, and how would you find out?

people.name: Mitsuye Endo
body: On July 12, 1942, a lawyer in San Francisco filed a habeas corpus petition in federal court on behalf of a 22-year-old Japanese American woman held behind barbed wire. Her case would reach the U.S. Supreme Court.

Endo was born May 10, 1920, in Sacramento, California, the second of four children of Japanese immigrant parents. She took a clerical job with the California Department of Employment. After Pearl Harbor, the State Personnel Board moved to dismiss Japanese American state workers, and by spring 1942 she had lost her job. She was one of 63 fired employees who challenged their dismissals with the help of the Japanese American Citizens League and attorney James C. Purcell.

She was held at the Sacramento Assembly Center, then at Tule Lake in California, and later at Topaz in Utah. When the government offered her an early release, she turned it down so the case could go forward. On December 18, 1944, the Supreme Court ruled in Ex parte Endo, in an opinion by Justice William O. Douglas with no dissents, that the War Relocation Authority had no authority to hold citizens it conceded were loyal. Just before the decision, which had been leaked to government officials, the Army opened the West Coast again to Japanese Americans it deemed loyal.

Endo left Topaz in May 1945 and moved to Chicago, where she worked as a secretary for the Mayor's Committee on Race Relations. About two years later she married Kenneth Tsutsumi, and they raised three children. By Densho's account she rarely spoke about the case. She died in Chicago on April 14, 2006. She was inducted into the California Hall of Fame in 2024, and on January 2, 2025, she was posthumously awarded the Presidential Citizens Medal.
keyFacts: 1920: Born May 10 in Sacramento, California.
1942: Fired from her state job; July 12 petition filed.
December 18, 1944: Supreme Court rules for her, with no dissents.
May 1945: Leaves Topaz for Chicago.
2006: Died April 14 in Chicago.
January 2, 2025: Posthumous Presidential Citizens Medal.
people.connectToWork: What does your process assume about people who turn down a quick fix because they want a fair result, and how would you treat that person's choice?

people.name: Daniel Ken Inouye
body: In 1943 a pre-med freshman at the University of Hawai'i enlisted in a new Army unit made up of soldiers of Japanese ancestry, the 442nd Regimental Combat Team. Two years later, in combat in Europe, Daniel Inouye lost his right arm. He came home with the Distinguished Service Cross, the Bronze Star and the Purple Heart. In June 2000 his Distinguished Service Cross was upgraded, and he was one of 22 Asian American World War II veterans awarded the Medal of Honor.
Inouye was born September 7, 1924, in Honolulu. The 442nd fought in Italy and France while many of its soldiers' families on the mainland were held in camps.

When Hawaii became a state in 1959, Inouye became the first Japanese American to serve in the U.S. House of Representatives. In 1962 he won election to the U.S. Senate, where he served until his death. He sat on the Senate Watergate Committee in 1973 and 1974, became the first chairman of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence in 1976, and chaired the special committee on the Iran-Contra affair from 1987 to 1989. He later chaired the Senate Appropriations Committee and the Select Committee on Indian Affairs.

In 2010 he became president pro tempore of the Senate, and he held that post until he died on December 17, 2012. In 2013 he was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom posthumously, the first senator to receive both that medal and the Medal of Honor.
keyFacts: 1924: Born September 7 in Honolulu.
1943: Enlisted in the 442nd Regimental Combat Team; lost his right arm in combat in 1945.
1959: First Japanese American in the U.S. House.
1962: Elected to the U.S. Senate.
June 2000: Awarded the Medal of Honor.
2010–2012: President pro tempore; died December 17, 2012.

people.name: Ellison Shoji Onizuka
body: In January 1985 the space shuttle Discovery lifted off on a classified Department of Defense mission. Aboard as a mission specialist was Ellison Onizuka, an Air Force engineer from Kona, Hawaii, whom the Challenger Center names as the first Asian American to go to space.

Onizuka was born June 24, 1946, in Kealakekua, Kona. He graduated with honors from Konawaena High School in 1964, where he was active in 4-H, student council, the Boy Scouts and varsity sports. At the University of Colorado he earned a B.S. in aeronautical engineering in 1968 and an M.S. in aerospace engineering in 1969, and he joined Air Force ROTC.

He entered the Air Force in January 1970 and worked as an aerospace flight test engineer at the Sacramento Air Logistics Center. In August 1974 he attended the Air Force Test Pilot School at Edwards Air Force Base, where he stayed as a squadron flight test officer and later as chief of its engineering support section.

In 1978 NASA chose him from about 8,000 applicants as one of 35 astronauts for the Space Shuttle program, the first Japanese American selected. After his 1985 flight, NASA assigned him to Challenger Flight 51-L. On January 28, 1986, the orbiter broke apart 73 seconds after liftoff, killing all seven crew members. In 2004 President George W. Bush awarded the Congressional Space Medal of Honor to Onizuka and his crewmates.
keyFacts: 1946: Born June 24 in Kealakekua, Kona, Hawaii.
1968 and 1969: B.S. and M.S., University of Colorado.
1978: Selected as a NASA astronaut, the first Japanese American chosen.
January 1985: First flight, aboard Discovery.
January 28, 1986: Died in the Challenger accident.
2004: Posthumous Congressional Space Medal of Honor.
people.connectToWork: When young people or families come to you from a small or rural place, what do you assume about what they can do, and what would you ask instead?

people.name: Yuri Kochiyama
body: On December 7, 1941, FBI agents took a San Pedro, California, father into custody. Seiichi Nakahara was held for six weeks and died on January 21, 1942, the day after he was released. His daughter would spend her long life fighting for people she believed were being treated unjustly. Densho and the UCLA Asian American Studies Center give her birth name as Mary Yuri Nakahara; the National Park Service and BlackPast give Mary Yuriko Nakahara.

She was born May 19, 1921, in San Pedro. After Executive Order 9066 her family was held first at the Santa Anita assembly center, in the racetrack's horse stables, and then for most of the war at the Jerome camp in Arkansas. At Jerome she wrote a camp newspaper column called "Nisei in Khaki," and her Sunday school group, the Crusaders, wrote letters to Japanese American soldiers. In 1944 she met one of them, Bill Kochiyama of the 442nd Regimental Combat Team, at a USO center in Hattiesburg, Mississippi. They married in New York City in 1946 and raised six children.

In 1960 the family moved to Harlem, and their apartment became a gathering place for activists and artists. Kochiyama joined the Harlem Parents Committee's school boycotts and was among 600 people arrested at a construction site protest demanding jobs for Black and Puerto Rican workers. In October 1963 she met Malcolm X, and she hosted him at her apartment in June 1964. She and her oldest son were in the audience at the Audubon Ballroom when he was assassinated on February 21, 1965.

In the 1980s she and Bill organized East Coast Japanese Americans for Redress and she testified before the federal Commission on Wartime Relocation and Internment of Civilians. She also championed ethnic studies and, after September 11, 2001, spoke out against Islamophobia. Her memoir, Passing It On, was published in 2004. She died June 1, 2014, in Berkeley, California, at age 93.
keyFacts: 1921: Born May 19 in San Pedro, California.
1942: Father died after FBI detention; family held at Santa Anita, then Jerome, Arkansas.
1946: Married Bill Kochiyama, a 442nd veteran.
1960: Moved to Harlem.
February 21, 1965: Present at the assassination of Malcolm X.
1980s: Organized for redress; testified before the federal commission.
2014: Died June 1 in Berkeley, California.
people.connectToWork: Who on your team could explain how the experience of one community has shaped its solidarity with another, and what would you need to learn before planning outreach that treats them as separate?

people.name: Yoshiko Dart
body: Yoshiko Dart, born Yoshiko Saji, is a first-generation Japanese American and a disability rights advocate. After graduating from Aoyama Gakuin University in Tokyo in 1963, she went to work for Tupperware Japan, then run by Justin Dart, and became his executive assistant before their marriage. The couple returned to Texas from Asia in 1978, shortly before Justin began his disability advocacy work.

Starting in 1988 they toured every state, plus Puerto Rico, Guam and Washington, D.C., to build support for the Americans with Disabilities Act. Their public forums drew more than 33,000 people, and they collected thousands of "discrimination diaries" that became part of the evidence for the law. In February 1990 she helped organize a Washington Post petition ad carrying more than 8,500 names. She also took many photographs of the movement.

When President Clinton awarded Justin the Presidential Medal of Freedom, he gave it straight to Yoshiko, saying it belonged to the whole movement. She has called the disability rights movement possibly "one of the last frontier movements in human development." She is an ally and organizer; the sources do not say she has a disability. In 2017 a Japanese disability organization described her supporting disability groups and youth programs, and in 2025 Access Press described her as still active.

1963: Graduated from Aoyama Gakuin University, Tokyo.
1978: Returned to Texas with Justin Dart.
1988 onward: ADA tour of all states, Puerto Rico, Guam and D.C.; more than 33,000 attendees.
1990: Helped organize a petition ad with more than 8,500 names.

people.name: Atsuko Kuwana
body: Atsuko Kuwana is a first-generation Japanese American and a wheelchair user, because of a spinal cord injury at birth. In February 1990 she was one of more than 8,500 people who signed a petition urging the House to pass the Americans with Disabilities Act, and she attended the July 26, 1990, signing at the White House with the Darts.

She married disability advocate Michael Winter, and they have an adopted son, Takayoshi Winter-Kuwana. Winter died in 2013, after 29 years of marriage. She returned to her hometown in Japan every year. In 2003 she spoke at an elementary school there and told the students that in America there are laws that protect people with disabilities so they can live and work together.
The Japan Times profiled her in 2019, reporting that she moved to Hawaii in 2015 and had taken up surfing and scuba diving.
keyFacts: Spinal cord injury at birth; uses a wheelchair.
1990: Signed the ADA petition and attended the signing.
2003: Spoke at a school in her hometown in Japan.
2015: Moved to Hawaii.
people.connectToWork: When someone has lived under two countries' disability systems, how would you ask what they expect from yours and what they have had to fight for elsewhere?

institutions.name: Twin Cities Japanese American Citizens League
aliases: Twin Cities chapter of the Japanese American Citizens League
Twin Cities Chapter, Japanese American Citizens League
body: On April 30, 1948, President Jon Matsuo called to order the first business meeting of a new organization at the downtown Minneapolis YWCA. By the chapter's own history, the group had begun forming in 1946, as Japanese Americans released from the camps and veterans of the Military Intelligence Service Language School settled in the Twin Cities. A Northwest Nisei article of Sept. 28, 1946, reprinted in the February 2026 Rice Paper, says the chapter was officially organized at an open meeting on Sept. 20, 1946, at the St. Paul International Institute, with about 200 people; that date is the basis for the 2026 80th anniversary. After debating a name in December 1946, members chose "United Citizens League" in 1947.

The group grew into a social and civic hub. Its records include a first golf tournament in 1959 and a biennial JACL district convention at Minneapolis's Radisson Hotel in 1961. On March 27, 1962, it took the name Twin Cities Japanese American Citizens League, formally part of the national JACL. By 1967 membership reached a record 261. The chapter incorporated as a Minnesota nonprofit on November 19, 1980, and in the 1980s it ran a mochi (rice cake) fundraiser that sold more than 1,000 pounds.

From the 1990s on, the chapter focused on preserving and teaching Japanese American civil rights history in the Twin Cities. In 2009 it sponsored an oral history project. Its education committee brings incarceration and Military Intelligence Service history to teacher conferences, offers curriculum guides and runs a speakers bureau. Its website also reposts the State of Minnesota's Discrimination Helpline, run by the Minnesota Department of Human Rights (1-833-454-0148, weekdays 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.), and in October 2026 it held an 80th anniversary Chrysanthemum Banquet.
keyFacts: September 20, 1946: Chapter officially organized at an open meeting at the St. Paul International Institute, with about 200 people.
1946: Chapter begins forming; named United Citizens League in 1947.
April 30, 1948: First business meeting at the downtown Minneapolis YWCA.
March 27, 1962: Renamed Twin Cities Japanese American Citizens League.
1967: Record membership of 261.
November 19, 1980: Incorporated as a Minnesota nonprofit.
October 2026: 80th anniversary banquet.

institutions.name: Normandale Japanese Garden
aliases: Normandale Japanese Garden (Friends of the Japanese Garden)
institutions.location: Normandale Community College, 9700 France Avenue South, Bloomington, Minnesota
body: In the early 1970s, a group of Japanese American veterans who had trained at the Military Intelligence Service Language School at Camp Savage and Fort Snelling paid for two of this Bloomington garden's best-known features: the Bentendo Pavilion and the Taikobashi Bridge. The college describes their gift as an expression of gratitude, cultural connection, reconciliation and commitment to peace between nations.

The garden began in 1964, when the Bloomington Affiliated Garden Clubs proposed it while the Normandale campus was still being built. The garden covers two acres. Takao Watanabe, a landscape architect for the Tokyo Metropolitan Government, donated the design. Ground was broken in 1972 and the garden was dedicated in 1976.

It is a Japanese strolling garden, meant to be walked through slowly. Volunteers known as the Friends of the Japanese Garden support its upkeep and events. The college and the City of Bloomington scheduled a free 50th anniversary celebration for September 19, 2026, with Japanese American and sister-city partners.
keyFacts: 1964: Proposed by the Bloomington Affiliated Garden Clubs.
Design donated by Takao Watanabe.
Early 1970s: Veterans fund the Bentendo Pavilion and Taikobashi Bridge.
1972: Groundbreaking; 1976: Dedication; two acres.
2026: 50th anniversary.

institutions.name: Japanese American National Museum
institutions.location: 100 North Central Avenue, Little Tokyo, Los Angeles, California
body: The Japanese American National Museum planned to open its doors on April 30, 1992. Days before, civil unrest broke out in Los Angeles, and the public opening moved to May 15. Its first home was the former Nishi Hongwanji Buddhist Temple building in Little Tokyo, which the city leased to it for $1 a year.

By Densho's account the museum was founded in 1982. Its first exhibition, Issei Pioneers: Hawai'i and the Mainland, 1885–1924, told the story of the first generation of Japanese immigrants. An early landmark exhibition, America's Concentration Camps: Remembering the Japanese American Experience, brought the incarceration to a wide public. On January 23, 1999, it opened its Pavilion, an 85,000-square-foot building designed by architect Gyo Obata.

It is an affiliate of the Smithsonian Institution and accredited by the American Alliance of Museums, and Densho reports that its building houses the world's largest collection of Japanese American artifacts. It also runs Discover Nikkei. As of October 2026 the Pavilion is closed for renovation, with reopening announced for January 23, 2027.
keyFacts: 1982: Founded.
May 15, 1992: Opened to the public in the former Nishi Hongwanji temple.
January 23, 1999: Pavilion opens.
Smithsonian affiliate; accredited by the American Alliance of Museums.
January 23, 2027: Announced reopening after renovation.

institutions.name: Keiro
institutions.location: Los Angeles, Orange and Ventura counties, California
body: In 1961 eight Japanese American community leaders in Los Angeles formed Keiro to buy the Japanese Hospital and provide care that respected the culture of Issei elders. It opened Keiro Nursing Home in 1969 and later added a retirement home, an intermediate care facility and a second nursing home. The Japanese Hospital closed in 1985.

As demand for its facilities fell and costs rose, Keiro sold them to Pacifica Companies. The sale was approved in 2015 and closed on February 5, 2016. Keiro now funds programs, classes and research for older adults and caregivers. In 2018 it described Iyashi Care, a palliative care program with Providence that works alongside a patient's own doctors, and an annual caregiver conference.

In May 2026, Cultural News reported that President and CEO Beverly Ito will retire at the end of 2026, in Keiro's 65th anniversary year, and described Keiro Kikyo Home, planned as a community-based care option for seniors. Keiro is not in Minnesota.
keyFacts: 1961: Founded by eight leaders.
1969: Nursing home opened.
1985: Japanese Hospital closed.
2016: Facilities sale closed; now runs community programs.
End of 2026: President and CEO Beverly Ito's announced retirement.
institutions.connectToWork: When a service is built by the people it serves and then changes hands, what would you ask about what stayed and what was lost?

institutions.name: Nikkei Concerns
body: In 1972 Japanese Americans in Seattle formed the Issei Concerns Committee. They had seen elders in mainstream nursing homes struggle to communicate, become isolated and eat poorly without familiar food. The group incorporated in 1976 and opened Seattle Keiro, a nursing facility, that September. It was renamed Nikkei Concerns in 1980 to serve all generations.

Its services grew to include the Kokoro Kai adult day program, begun in 1977, and Nikkei Manor assisted living, opened in 1998. It describes its values as including respect, trust and kimochi, which it translates as "good feelings." The organization was renamed Keiro Northwest in 2016, and the original Seattle Keiro nursing home closed in 2019. As of its 50th anniversary in 2025, Keiro Northwest continued Nikkei Manor and Kokoro Kai.
keyFacts: 1972: Founded as the Issei Concerns Committee.
1976: Incorporated; Seattle Keiro opened.
1980: Renamed Nikkei Concerns.
1998: Nikkei Manor opened.
2016: Renamed Keiro Northwest.
2019: Original nursing home closed.

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Here, Japanese American covers later-generation families whose history includes wartime incarceration and resettlement, more recent immigrants from Japan, mixed-heritage families, and Japanese nationals here for work or study. Language, ties to Japan and religious practice vary widely across them. We did not find a Minnesota study of how Japanese Americans understand disability. The studies below come from Japan, from cross-national work with educators, or from caregivers of older adults, not people with lifelong disabilities.
questions: What words do you use for your disability or your family member's situation?
Has anyone given you a diagnosis or a label? Has it helped or got in the way?
What would you want a disability label or assessment to open up for you? Is there anything you want it to avoid?
How long has your family been in the United States, and what would you like me to know about that?
Which language do you want to use with me, and would you like an interpreter or written materials in Japanese?
Who in your family helps make care decisions, and who would you like included?
Are you also caring for someone else, including a relative in Japan?
What makes a service feel comfortable for you, such as food, language, staff background or community connections?
Would respite or help at home make a difference for you? What would you want to know before trying it?
Have past experiences with government systems shaped how you feel about this process? Is there anything you would like me to know?
Do you belong to a temple, church or community group that you would like connected to your services, or would you rather keep them separate?
If you would like to tell me, what do you understand about how your disability came about?

context.heading: Stigma and shame: what studies looked at
body: A 2017 interview study asked school educators in Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and the United States how stigma affects their work with parents of children with disabilities. Educators in all four countries said it strained their relationships with parents. Japanese educators described quietly watching over and guiding parents, with empathy, while US educators described fact-based, solution-focused responses (Kayama and colleagues). It studied educators in those countries, not Japanese American families.

A Review of Disability Studies forum on shame and disability (Patterson, Baker and Jones) says shame is shaped by many factors, from the wider culture to family dynamics, and notes that after the 2016 Tsukui Lily Garden attack in Japan many victims' families asked not to be named. Do not read shame into a family because of its heritage.

sources.label: Kayama, Haight, Ku, Cho and Lee, Children and Youth Services Review 73 (2017)
Patterson, Baker and Jones, Disability and Shame, Review of Disability Studies, Vol. 15, Issue 3

context.heading: Family care across generations and borders
body: A University of Washington dissertation studied 40 Chinese American and Japanese American family caregivers of older adults, from the second, "2.5" and third generations. Later-generation caregivers were more acculturated yet still reported filial responsibility, and stayed involved after a relative moved into long-term care. In California survey data, third-generation Asian caregivers used respite care the least (Miyawaki, 2014). The study was about elder care and did not establish why. Offer respite and in-home support early and explain them plainly, and do not read low use as lack of need.

A 2021 conference abstract reported interviews with 20 Japanese Americans aged 40 to 59 in California who care for parents in Japan. Pandemic travel limits caused distress and, for some, relief, and support shifted to emotional and financial help given online (Hoshino, Tseng and Kamide). It is a small sample from one state.

sources.label: Miyawaki (2014), University of Washington dissertation
Hoshino, Tseng and Kamide, Innovation in Aging 5(S1) (2021)

context.heading: Care built by the people it serves
body: Keiro in Los Angeles and Nikkei Concerns in Seattle, both described on this page, are documented cases of Japanese Americans building their own care. By HistoryLink's account, Nikkei Concerns began after Issei elders in mainstream nursing homes struggled to communicate, became isolated and ate poorly without familiar food. In Minnesota, Cha-Ami Japanese Cultural Center runs a newer aging services program for Japanese American seniors and caregivers, listed below. Ask what would make a service comfortable rather than assuming it.

context.heading: What we could not find
body: We found no research on Japanese American beliefs about the causes of disability, no source on Japanese-language disability terms as used by Japanese Americans, and none on how families combine faith practices with disability services. No terms are offered here. Some people belong to Buddhist temples or Christian churches, and many do not, so ask. For people who prefer Japanese, use a qualified interpreter rather than a family member.

We also found no Japanese-specific disability agency in Minnesota. The Twin Cities JACL is a community contact, not a disability service, and wartime incarceration may shape how a person feels about government systems. Let them raise it.

communityRoutes.name: Cha-Ami Aging Services
communityRoutes.purpose: Volunteer help such as grocery delivery, chores and social visits, classes on health conditions, medical directives, housing and caregiver self-care, and twice-monthly Wa no Kai gatherings, for Japanese American seniors and their caregivers. Partly funded by the Minnesota DHS Live Well at Home program, whose state fiscal year 2025 grantee list shows a $52,000 award to Cha-Ami. Confirm the current address with Cha-Ami; its website gives a P.O. Box in Champlin, and the DHS list places it in St. Paul.

communityRoutes.name: Minnesota Discrimination Helpline (posted by the Twin Cities JACL)
communityRoutes.purpose: The State of Minnesota's Discrimination Helpline, launched April 6, 2020, by the governor and lieutenant governor and run by the Minnesota Department of Human Rights (1-833-454-0148, weekdays 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.). The Twin Cities chapter of the Japanese American Citizens League reposts it with talking points from the Coalition of Asian American Leaders; it is not a JACL-run helpline and not a disability service.

organizations.intro: Minnesota's Japanese community has at least two parts: a long-settled Japanese American community whose roots go back to the wartime Military Intelligence Service Language School and to resettlement from the camps, and a newer group of Japanese nationals and families, many tied to Japanese companies here. People gather through civil rights and heritage groups, friendship and business associations, Saturday schools, cultural sites and faith communities. The list below is not complete, and listing here says nothing about who a person trusts.

entries.purpose: A member-supported nonprofit founded in 1972 that promotes U.S.–Japan understanding. Runs the Mondale Award and Scholarship Gala, scheduled for November 14, 2026, and J-Quiz, and supports Minnesota's sister-city ties, two Saturday Japanese schools and, by its count, more than 100 Japanese corporate subsidiaries in the state.

It received a $25,000 Minnesota Arts and Cultural Heritage grant for 2024 and 2025. The DHS Live Well at Home grantee list for state fiscal year 2025 shows a $52,000 award to Cha-Ami.
